growth_story.headline: Belgium's income per person has grown about 1.3 percent a year since 1990, as productivity gains faded and costs, ageing and debt pressed on an open economy.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Belgium's income per person has grown by 1.3 percent a year on average, with no lasting shift up or down: the data show one long era. Within it the pace eased: there were years of 3.5 percent growth in 1997 and 2000, but 2006-2015 averaged only 0.6 percent, with a fall of 2.7 percent in 2009 and small declines in 2012 and 2013. The OECD says productivity growth has slowed since the 1990s, more than in other rich economies, and links this to weak business dynamism and the slow spread of technology; by 2010 Belgian wages had also drifted above those of its neighbours, a gap that wage restraint later closed. Growth picked up to 1.0 percent a year over 2016-2025, through a drop of 5.2 percent in 2020 and rebounds of 5.8 and 3.2 percent in 2021 and 2022. The IMF and OECD describe an economy that came through the pandemic and the energy crisis well, with wage indexation protecting household spending, but that was left with larger deficits, rising public debt and weaker price competitiveness. Since then growth has been slow, at 0.7, 0.4 and 0.3 percent in 2023, 2024 and 2025, though income per person in 2025 was the highest on record.

threads.title: A long productivity slowdown
threads.text: Belgium's productivity is high, but its growth has slowed since the 1990s. The OECD points to few firms entering and leaving markets and to new technology spreading slowly from leading firms to the rest. The IMF reports productivity growth still sluggish in 2025.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Belgium 2024
citations.quote: Productivity growth has slowed significantly since the 1990's, more than in other advanced economies, though it does remain high in level terms.

citations.title: Belgium: 2026 Article IV Consultation - Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Belgium (IMF Country Report No. 26/49)
citations.quote: Labor-productivity growth remained sluggish, but declining wage growth in 2024-25H1 brought overall unit labor cost increases since 2021 closer to the EA average.

threads.title: Wage costs and the neighbours
threads.text: Belgian wages follow prices automatically, and a law sets wage growth against France, Germany and the Netherlands. By 2010 Belgian wages had risen faster than in those countries; low wage norms in the early 2010s and a pause in indexation in 2015-16 closed the gap, in a decade (2006-2015) when income per person grew only 0.6 percent a year.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Belgium 2024
citations.quote: By 2010 a 4% gap had emerged between salary developments in Belgium and the comparator countries of Germany, France, and the Netherlands

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Belgium 2024
citations.quote: This led to a closing of the labour cost gap and greater cost competitiveness (IMF, 2019).

threads.title: Pandemic, energy shock and debt
threads.text: Income per person fell 5.2 percent in 2020 and recovered quickly in 2021 and 2022. Wage indexation and energy support protected household spending power through the energy crisis, but the two shocks left larger deficits, higher public debt and weaker price competitiveness, which still weigh on the outlook.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Belgium 2024
citations.quote: Automatic wage indexation and energy-related support measures helped preserve household purchasing power.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Belgium 2024
citations.quote: The pandemic and the energy crisis have left Belgium with higher structural deficits and a further increase in an already high debt-to-GDP ratio.

citations.title: Belgium: 2026 Article IV Consultation - Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Belgium (IMF Country Report No. 26/49)
citations.quote: Belgium emerged from the pandemic and energy crisis with large structural fiscal deficits, an elevated and rising public debt, a deteriorated price-competitiveness

threads.title: Ageing and too few workers
threads.text: An ageing population is slowing the growth of the workforce, and the OECD notes large employment gaps for women, older people and other groups. Recent reforms have drawn more people into the labour force, which pushed unemployment up.

citations.title: Belgium: 2026 Article IV Consultation - Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Belgium (IMF Country Report No. 26/49)
citations.quote: With population aging weighing on employment growth, raising productivity and labor-force participation is paramount

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Belgium 2024

citations.title: Belgium: 2026 Article IV Consultation - Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Belgium (IMF Country Report No. 26/49)
citations.quote: The rise in unemployment reflected an increase in labor force participation following government reforms

threads.title: An open economy facing headwinds
threads.text: Belgium is highly exposed to slow world trade, and wage indexation has eroded exporters' price competitiveness. Its industry faces a large energy-cost gap with rivals in the United States and China, and the IMF expects higher US tariffs to hold back growth.

growth_story.tension: The IMF calls activity solid and the OECD calls the economy resilient, yet income per person grew only 0.7, 0.4 and 0.3 percent in 2023, 2024 and 2025. In the other direction, the OECD describes subdued productivity gains over the past decade, while income per person grew faster in 2016-2025 (1.0 percent a year) than in 2006-2015 (0.6), a decade that held the 2009 fall.
